newsitem.title: UK: Banks to struggle as EMU stokes currency volatility.
newsitem.headline: Banks to struggle as EMU stokes currency volatility.

text.p: The drive for European economic and monetary union (EMU) will create significant volatility on currency markets this year and leaner, meaner foreign exchange operations may struggle to cope, senior traders at British banks say.

"The EMS currencies will definitely be volatile but that will lead on to the dollar and sterling being volatile as well because they're haven-type currencies," Dave White, chief dealer, foreign exchange at NatWest Markets in London, said in an interview.
Volatility shrank to record lows last year as market players flocked into so-called convergence trades, based on the expectation that European economies will dovetail in the run-up to EMU.
But as the proposed January 1, 1999, start date for currency union draws nearer, the landscape could look very different.

"We might be in for a period of volatility in the forex markets, maybe akin to 1992/93, and as an industry we're not geared up for it, because all we've done is lay people off," said the deputy head of currency trading at a major British bank, who declined to be identified.
"It will add to volatility, the fact there are fewer people out there," he added.

Sterling and the Italian lira crashed out of Europe's exchange rate mechanism in September 1992 and a period of pronounced market volatility came to a head the following August, when the trading bands within which most member currencies were allowed to fluctuate were expanded to 15 percent from 2.25.

Almost four years on, the markets are jittery as they contemplate the launch of a European single currency. Convergence plays may have been the hottest trades in town last year but that does not guarantee a smooth run-up to 1999.

"Anyone who's not prepared for volatility in EMS (European Monetary System) currencies over the next couple of years should think again. Surely the uncertainty means there's going to be a lot of shifting in and out of European currencies," said the deputy head of currency trading.
The advent of EMU has been blamed for much of the downsizing seen on foreign exchange trading desks in recent times. But NatWest's White said further savage job cuts were unlikely.
"I think we'll see the continuation of quality people being employed in quality areas," he said. "The amount of people in the business is right but the quality of the people is not necessarily right.
"The banks that have let their experienced people go and employed younger guys to cover it may struggle."

The first weeks of 1997 have seen vibrant currency markets, with the dollar surging to its strongest levels in years and mark weakness across the board a growing feature -- both trends which the dealers expect to continue.

The dollar's inexorable rise has set the market fretting over the possibility of central bank intervention. But dealers question just how effective the authorities could be and the implications for market volatility.
"There's a sense that central banks are losing their stranglehold on the market...last year they were really in control of the market," said the deputy head of forex.
"To get real volatility, you need central banks to no longer be in control."
